newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania king, citizenship restored, to visit home.
newsitem.headline: Romania king, citizenship restored, to visit home.

text.p: Romania's exiled King Michael, his citizenship restored by the country's new centrist authorities, is to visit his homeland this week for the first time since a triumphant return five years ago, his office said.

A statement issued on Monday by Michael's office in the Swiss town of Versoix -- three days after his citizenship was returned -- said Michael would arrive on Friday for a "first stay" of five days in Bucharest.
It gave no indication whether Michael, forced into exile by communists in 1947, would meet President Emil Constantinescu.

But he thanked Romania's new leaders, who ousted ex-communists in November elections, for allowing the visit to take place "and re-establishing democracy in our country. The anticipation felt throughout my life has been vindicated.
"I am coming not to take but to give, not to divide but to unite. I am coming to help, through my efforts combined with yours to rid Romania of its past miseries and tragic events."

Michael, 75, is respected for breaking Romania's World War Two alliance with Nazi Germany in 1944 and switching his allegiance to the Allies. He was dethroned by Moscow-backed communists who seized power after Soviet troops occupied Romania at the close of the war.

Michael's status became an issue during the November campaign, when President Ion Iliescu accused his right-of-centre rivals of wanting to restore the monarchy and overturn the post-communist republican constitution.
In his message, Michael said his oath obliged him to refrain during his visit from raising constitutional or "material" issues -- meaning claims to confiscated property.
Michael is to lay a wreath in University Square, where dozens of people died in the 1989 upheaval, and attend a service at the Romanian Orthodox church's main cathedral.

Government officials were unavailable for comment on the visit. But the National Peasant Party, the main group within the ruling coalition, described the visit as private and praised it as a "natural event after a long and unjust exile".

During his first visit in 1992, three years after the execution of communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, the king was greeted by hundreds of thousands of well-wishers who poured into Bucharest streets at Orthodox Easter.
But a subsequent attempt to return was thwarted by the former leftist government and by Iliescu, who insisted that he must first abandon all claims to the throne.

Two small monarchist parties function in Romania, one within the ruling coalition and only a small fraction of Romanians favour restoration of the king. But Michael's personal appeal may go far beyond political considerations.
